breakdown.whatIsIt: The Operators Final Challenge is a milestone synthesis applying arithmetic, assignment, relational, logical, ternary, and bitwise operators to a real-world enterprise problem.

questions.prompt: What is the value of: int a = 5; int b = ++a * 2 - a--; ?
questions.question: What is the value of: int a = 5; int b = ++a * 2 - a--; ?
questions.explanation: ++a makes a=6 and evaluates to 6. 6 * 2 is 12. Then a-- evaluates to 6 (and decrements a to 5). 12 - 6 = 6.

questions.prompt: What will be printed: int x = 0; if (x != 0 && 10 / x > 2) { System.out.print("A"); } else { System.out.print("B"); }
questions.question: What will be printed: int x = 0; if (x != 0 && 10 / x > 2) { System.out.print("A"); } else { System.out.print("B"); }
questions.explanation: x != 0 is false. Due to short-circuit evaluation with &&, 10 / x is skipped. The else branch executes and prints B.
hints: && short-circuits when left side is false.

questions.prompt: What is the value of status: int score = 85; String status = (score >= 90) ? "A" : (score >= 80) ? "B" : "C"; ?
questions.question: What is the value of status: int score = 85; String status = (score >= 90) ? "A" : (score >= 80) ? "B" : "C"; ?
questions.explanation: score >= 90 is false, so it evaluates the false branch: (score >= 80) ? "B" : "C". Since 85 >= 80 is true, it yields "B".
hints: Check the first condition, then proceed to the inner branch.

questions.prompt: What is the result of: int n = 7; int res = (n & 1) == 0 ? (n >> 1) : (n << 1); ?
questions.question: What is the result of: int n = 7; int res = (n & 1) == 0 ? (n >> 1) : (n << 1); ?
questions.explanation: 7 is odd, so (7 & 1) is 1, meaning (7 & 1) == 0 is false. The false branch executes: 7 << 1 (7 * 2 = 14).
hints: 7 is odd, so the condition is false. 7 << 1 doubles 7.

activities.title: Top Placement Interview Questions: Operators Capstone

interviewQA.question: Summarize the 3 most common operator bugs every junior Java developer must avoid.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer:
1. Integer division truncation: `17 / 20` becoming `0` instead of `0.85`.
2. Assignment in if condition: `if (isMember = true)` instead of `==`.
3. Side-effects in short-circuited logic: `if (flag && count++ > 0)` where `count++` might never run.
keyPoints: Avoid integer division truncation, = vs == confusion, and side effects in short circuits.

interviewQA.question: Why should parentheses always be used even when operator precedence is well known?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Because code is read far more often than it is written. Explicit parentheses communicate developer intent unambiguously, reduce cognitive overhead during code reviews, and eliminate risks of subtle bugs when expressions are refactored by other team members.
keyPoints: Parentheses document developer intent and make maintenance bug-free.

interviewQA.question: How does Java handle operator overloading?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Unlike C++, Java does NOT allow user-defined operator overloading. The only operator overloaded by the language itself is `+`, which performs numeric addition for numbers and string concatenation when at least one operand is a `String`.
keyPoints: Java does not support custom operator overloading; only + is built-in overloaded for Strings.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between bitwise & and logical &&?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: `&&` short-circuits (skips right-hand evaluation if left is false) and operates strictly on booleans. `&` always evaluates both sides unconditionally and can operate on both booleans and integer binary bit patterns.
keyPoints: && short-circuits and is boolean-only; & evaluates both sides and supports bit manipulation.

interviewQA.question: Can the ternary operator be used as a standalone statement without assigning its result?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. In Java, the ternary operator is strictly an expression that must produce a value used in an assignment, return statement, or method argument (e.g. `(a > b) ? x : y;` as a standalone line will not compile).
keyPoints: Ternary is an expression that must return a value; it cannot stand alone like an if statement.
